title: Buffer solutions
summary: A [[buffer-solution|buffer solution]] holds its [[ph|pH]] almost steady when a little acid or alkali is added. It contains a [[weak-acid|weak acid]] and its conjugate base (or a [[weak-base|weak base]] and its conjugate acid), both in large amounts: one partner removes added $\ce{H^+}$, the other added $\ce{OH^-}$. Its pH is set by the [[pka|pKa]] and the ratio of the two concentrations.

goals.text: State what acidic and basic buffers contain, and make one by partly neutralizing a weak acid or weak base.
Explain, with equations, how a buffer resists a change in pH, and why it must be made from a weak conjugate pair.
Calculate the pH of a buffer from its pKa or pKb and the concentration ratio, and the composition needed for a target pH.
Explain why diluting a buffer leaves its pH almost unchanged.

synonyms: effect of dilution on a buffer

before.prompt: A weak acid has $K_\mathrm{a} = \pu{1.8e-5 mol dm-3}$ at 298 K. What is its pKa, to 2 decimal places?
A system is at equilibrium: $\ce{A(aq) <=> B(aq) + C(aq)}$. More C is added. What happens?
before.hint: The system responds to oppose the change.

options.text: The position shifts left, using up some of the added C
The position shifts right, making more C
Nothing changes, because the system is already at equilibrium
The equilibrium constant increases

before.explain: The position moves left to remove some of the added C; the constant itself is unchanged. Revise it in {{lesson:5.9}}.

verify.truth: The position shifts left, using up some of the added C

before.prompt: Which of these is a weak base?
before.hint: A weak base only partly reacts with water to make hydroxide ions.

options.text: ammonia
sodium hydroxide
potassium chloride
ethanoic acid

before.explain: Ammonia reacts with only a small fraction of water molecules; sodium hydroxide is a strong base. Revise it in {{lesson:6.3}}.

sections.heading: What a buffer is and how it works

blocks.text: One drop of concentrated hydrochloric acid takes a litre of pure water from pH 7 to about 3. Blood can't cope with swings like that.

blocks.statement: A solution whose pH changes very little when a small amount of acid or alkali is added to it.

blocks.text: An acidic buffer (usually pH below 7) is a [[weak-acid|weak acid]] mixed with a salt of its conjugate base, such as ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate. It holds lots of $\ce{CH3COOH}$ and lots of $\ce{CH3COO^-}$, a [[conjugate-acid-base-pair|conjugate acid–base pair]] ({{lesson:6.1}}).
A basic buffer (usually pH above 7) is a [[weak-base|weak base]] mixed with a salt of its conjugate acid, such as ammonia with ammonium chloride.
Write a weak acid as HA: $\ce{HA(aq) <=> H^+(aq) + A^-(aq)}$. On its own, HA barely ionizes, so there is very little $\ce{A^-}$. The salt supplies a large amount of it.

blocks.alt: Buffer action. At the top is the equilibrium HA, reversible arrow, H plus plus A minus. HA is labelled large amount, H plus is labelled tiny, and A minus is labelled large amount. An arrow runs down from HA to a box on the left headed: add a little OH minus. It shows HA plus OH minus gives A minus plus water, and says the added OH minus is used up. An arrow runs down from A minus to a box on the right headed: add a little H plus. It shows A minus plus H plus gives HA, and says the added H plus is used up.
blocks.caption: Each partner removes one kind of addition. The ratio of HA to $\ce{A^-}$ changes only a little, so the pH does too.

blocks.text: Add a little acid and the conjugate base removes the $\ce{H^+}$: $\ce{A^-(aq) + H^+(aq) -> HA(aq)}$. Add a little alkali and the weak acid removes the $\ce{OH^-}$: $\ce{HA(aq) + OH^-(aq) -> A^-(aq) + H2O(l)}$.

In terms of [[le-chateliers-principle|Le Châtelier's principle]]: added $\ce{H^+}$ shifts $\ce{HA <=> H^+ + A^-}$ to the left, using the large store of $\ce{A^-}$. Added $\ce{OH^-}$ removes $\ce{H^+}$, so the position shifts right and the large store of HA replaces it.
In a basic buffer, $\ce{NH3 + H^+ -> NH4^+}$ removes added acid and $\ce{NH4^+ + OH^- -> NH3 + H2O}$ removes added alkali.

Why weak? A [[strong-acid|strong acid]] such as HCl is fully ionized, and $\ce{Cl^-}$ is far too weak a base to take back a proton. So nothing in HCl and NaCl removes added $\ce{H^+}$. Likewise, in a [[strong-base|strong base]] and its salt, $\ce{Na^+}$ can't give up a proton.
A buffer copes with small additions only, and works best when both partners are present in large, similar amounts.

You can also add a strong base to an excess of weak acid: part of the acid becomes $\ce{A^-}$ and the rest stays as HA. This is the [[buffer-region|buffer region]] of a pH curve ({{lesson:6.5}}). A strong acid added to excess weak base makes a basic buffer.

blocks.question: A buffer contains propanoic acid, $\ce{CH3CH2COOH}$, and sodium propanoate. Write the equation for the reaction that removes a small amount of added hydroxide ions.
steps: Pick the partner that reacts with a base: the weak acid, $\ce{CH3CH2COOH}$.
It gives its proton to $\ce{OH^-}$, forming its conjugate base and water.
Check: atoms and charge balance. Sodium ions are spectators, so leave them out.

blocks.question: A student mixes hydrochloric acid with sodium chloride solution and calls it a buffer. Explain why it is not a buffer.
steps: A buffer needs a partner for each kind of addition.
Ask what in the mixture could remove added $\ce{H^+}$.
Finish by saying what a buffer needs instead.
blocks.answer: A buffer needs a base to remove added $\ce{H^+}$ and an acid to remove added $\ce{OH^-}$. Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, so it is fully ionized. Its conjugate base, $\ce{Cl^-}$, is too weak a base to accept a proton. So any added $\ce{H^+}$ stays in solution, and the pH falls. A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base, both present in large amounts.

verify.truth: HCl is strong and fully ionized; Cl- is too weak a base to accept H+, so added H+ is not removed; a buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base.
requires: weak acid and its conjugate base

blocks.text: Calling any acid plus its salt a buffer. The acid must be weak, so that both it and its conjugate base can react.

blocks.prompt: A buffer contains ammonia and ammonium chloride. Which equation shows how it removes a small amount of added acid?
blocks.hint: Which partner can accept a proton?

options.text: $\ce{Cl^- + H^+ -> HCl}$

blocks.explain: Ammonia, the weak base, accepts the proton. The second equation removes added alkali, and chloride is too weak a base.

blocks.hint: A buffer needs weak acid left over, as well as its conjugate base.

options.text: 30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid with 15.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ KOH
30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid with 30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ KOH
30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid with 15.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ KOH
30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid with 15.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ KOH

blocks.explain: Each has $\pu{0.00600 mol}$ of acid. Only the first adds less base ($\pu{0.00300 mol}$), leaving half as HA and half as its conjugate base. The next two neutralize it all, and the last uses a strong acid.

verify.truth: 30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid with 15.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ KOH

sections.heading: Calculating the pH of a buffer

blocks.text: Start from the [[acid-dissociation-constant|acid dissociation constant]] of the weak acid ({{lesson:6.4}}). It is an [[equilibrium-constant|equilibrium constant]], so it holds in any solution containing HA, including a buffer.
Take $-\log_{10}$ of both sides. The log of a product is a sum of logs, and flipping the fraction changes the sign of its log.
This is the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. It is not in the data booklet, so learn it, or work from $K_\mathrm{a}$ each time. Mark schemes accept either route.
Use the concentrations you put in. With so much $\ce{A^-}$ present, HA ionizes even less than usual, and [[salt-hydrolysis|salt hydrolysis]] of $\ce{A^-}$ is negligible too.
Both species share one volume, so the ratio of their [[molar-concentration|molar concentrations]] equals the ratio of their [[mole|moles]]. Amounts can go straight into the fraction.

So the pH depends on the pKa and on the ratio $[\ce{A^-}]:[\ce{HA}]$. When they are equal, $\log_{10}1 = 0$ and $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$. For a target pH, choose an acid with a pKa close to it, then adjust the ratio.

For a basic buffer of base B and its conjugate acid $\ce{BH^+}$, use the [[base-dissociation-constant|base dissociation constant]] in the same way: $\mathrm{pOH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b} + \log_{10}\frac{[\ce{BH^+}]}{[\ce{B}]}$. Then $\mathrm{pH} = 14.00 - \mathrm{pOH}$ at 298 K, using $K_\mathrm{w}$ from the data booklet (section 2).

blocks.question: A buffer contains $\pu{0.150 mol dm-3}$ benzoic acid and $\pu{0.240 mol dm-3}$ sodium benzoate. The pKa of benzoic acid is 4.20 at 298 K. Calculate the pH of the buffer.
steps: The conjugate base is the benzoate ion, so $[\ce{A^-}] = \pu{0.240 mol dm-3}$ and $[\ce{HA}] = \pu{0.150 mol dm-3}$.
Check: more conjugate base than acid, so the pH is a little above the pKa.

blocks.question: $\pu{24.0 cm3}$ of $\pu{0.125 mol dm-3}$ sodium hydroxide is added to $\pu{35.0 cm3}$ of $\pu{0.300 mol dm-3}$ propanoic acid. The pKa of propanoic acid is 4.87 at 298 K. Calculate the pH of the mixture.
steps: The hydroxide reacts completely: $\ce{CH3CH2COOH + OH^- -> CH3CH2COO^- + H2O}$. This leaves $0.0105 - 0.00300 = \pu{0.00750 mol}$ of acid and makes $\pu{0.00300 mol}$ of propanoate.
Weak acid and conjugate base are both present, so this is a buffer. Use moles in the ratio: $\mathrm{pH} = 4.87 + \log_{10}\frac{0.00300}{0.00750} = 4.87 - 0.398$.
Check: less conjugate base than acid, so the pH is below the pKa.

blocks.text: Turning the ratio upside down. The conjugate base goes on top: $\log_{10}\frac{[\ce{A^-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}$. Check the direction: more conjugate base means a pH above the pKa.

blocks.prompt: A basic buffer contains $\pu{0.180 mol dm-3}$ methylamine and $\pu{0.300 mol dm-3}$ methylammonium chloride. The pKb of methylamine is 3.36 at 298 K. What is the pH, to 2 decimal places?
blocks.hint: Find the pOH with pKb and $\frac{[\ce{BH^+}]}{[\ce{B}]}$, then subtract it from 14.00.

blocks.prompt: A buffer is made from a weak acid HA with a pKa of 6.80. Its pH is 7.10. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: Compare the pH with the pKa. What sign must $\log_{10}\frac{[\ce{A^-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}$ have?

options.text: There is more conjugate base than weak acid
There are equal amounts of weak acid and conjugate base
There is more weak acid than conjugate base

blocks.explain: The pH is above the pKa, so the log term is positive and $\frac{[\ce{A^-}]}{[\ce{HA}]} > 1$. Equal concentrations would give $\mathrm{pH} = 6.80$.

verify.truth: There is more conjugate base than weak acid

blocks.prompt: A buffer of pH 4.10 must contain $\pu{0.0800 mol dm-3}$ lactic acid, which has a pKa of 3.86 at 298 K. What concentration of sodium lactate is needed, in $\pu{mol dm-3}$ to 3 significant figures?

blocks.text: Under [[dilution|dilution]] with water, $[\ce{HA}]$ and $[\ce{A^-}]$ fall by the same factor, so their ratio is unchanged. $K_\mathrm{a}$ depends only on temperature, so the pH stays almost the same. A weak acid on its own is different: diluting it tenfold raises its pH by about 0.5.

In Le Châtelier terms, dilution favours the side of $\ce{HA <=> H^+ + A^-}$ with more dissolved particles. The position shifts right, and the extra ionization replaces the $\ce{H^+}$ that dilution spread out.
The cost: each $\pu{cm3}$ now holds less HA and $\ce{A^-}$, so it absorbs less added acid or alkali. After enormous dilution the pH drifts towards 7.

blocks.question: A buffer of propanoic acid and sodium propanoate is diluted with an equal volume of water at constant temperature. Explain the effect on its pH.
steps: Link the ratio and the constant to the pH, one point per sentence.
blocks.answer: Adding water halves both $[\ce{CH3CH2COOH}]$ and $[\ce{CH3CH2COO^-}]$, so both fall by the same factor. The ratio of conjugate base to acid is therefore unchanged. At constant temperature $K_\mathrm{a}$, and so the pKa, does not change. Since $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} + \log_{10}\frac{[\ce{A^-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}$, the pH stays almost the same.

verify.truth: Both concentrations fall by the same factor, so the ratio is unchanged; Ka is constant at constant temperature; so the pH stays almost the same.

blocks.question: $\pu{100.0 cm3}$ of a buffer contains $\pu{0.150 mol dm-3}$ ethanoic acid and $\pu{0.150 mol dm-3}$ sodium ethanoate. The pKa of ethanoic acid is 4.76 at 298 K. Calculate the pH after $\pu{0.500 cm3}$ of $\pu{2.00 mol dm-3}$ hydrochloric acid is added.
steps: It reacts with ethanoate: $\ce{CH3COO^- + H^+ -> CH3COOH}$. Now $n(\ce{CH3COO^-}) = \pu{0.0140 mol}$ and $n(\ce{CH3COOH}) = \pu{0.0160 mol}$.
$\mathrm{pH} = 4.76 + \log_{10}\frac{0.0140}{0.0160} = 4.76 - 0.058$: a fall of only 0.06. In pure water the same acid would drop the pH from 7 to about 2.

blocks.text: When acid or alkali is added to a buffer, work in moles: react the addition with the right partner first, then put the new amounts into the ratio.

blocks.prompt: A buffer of pH 5.20 is diluted with water to ten times its volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pH?
blocks.hint: What happens to the ratio of the two concentrations?

options.text: It stays almost the same
It rises by about one unit
It falls by about one unit
It becomes neutral

blocks.explain: Both concentrations fall tenfold, so the ratio is unchanged and the pH stays about 5.20.

blocks.prompt: A small amount of sodium hydroxide is added to a buffer of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: Which partner reacts with hydroxide ions, and what does it make?

options.text: The ethanoate ion concentration increases slightly
The ethanoic acid concentration increases slightly
Hydroxide ions combine with sodium ions to form sodium hydroxide
The pH stays exactly the same

blocks.explain: $\ce{CH3COOH + OH^- -> CH3COO^- + H2O}$ uses up a little acid and makes a little more ethanoate. The pH rises very slightly: a buffer resists change, it doesn't stop it.

verify.truth: The ethanoate ion concentration increases slightly

blocks.text: Acidic buffer: weak acid plus a salt of its conjugate base. Basic buffer: weak base plus a salt of its conjugate acid. Both in large amounts.
Buffer action: $\ce{A^- + H^+ -> HA}$ removes added acid; $\ce{HA + OH^- -> A^- + H2O}$ removes added alkali. Strong acids and bases can't buffer.
Basic buffer: $\mathrm{pOH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b} + \log_{10}\frac{[\ce{BH^+}]}{[\ce{B}]}$, then $\mathrm{pH} = 14.00 - \mathrm{pOH}$ at 298 K.
$[\ce{HA}] = [\ce{A^-}]$ gives $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$. Strong base plus excess weak acid makes a buffer.
Dilution leaves the ratio, so the pH, almost unchanged.

mistakes: Adding too much strong base when making a buffer. If all the weak acid is neutralized, only the salt is left; keep the weak acid in excess.
Stopping at the pOH for a basic buffer. Finish with pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Saying a buffer keeps the pH constant. It resists change: the pH moves a little, and a large addition overwhelms it.
Thinking dilution changes a buffer's pH as it does a weak acid's. The ratio stays the same, so the pH barely moves.
examTips: "Describe" a buffer: name the weak acid (or base) and its conjugate base (or acid), both present in large amounts.
Equations for buffer action: give one for added $\ce{H^+}$ and one for added $\ce{OH^-}$, using the buffer's own species.
"Calculate" a buffer pH: write the expression, substitute, and give the pH to 2 decimal places.
